transcript.reader:
Let me check I have your strongest version before I touch anything. You're saying: the Internet had no Grand Plan, it grew by evolution with rough consensus and running code, and the principles that survived are — one IP at the internet layer, independent of hardware and hardware addressing; intelligence end-to-end rather than in the network, with the network keeping only minimal, self-healing state (so datagrams beat virtual circuits); and no central control, nobody able to turn it off. Have I got that right, and is the claim we're testing *why the architecture came out this way*, or *what a protocol designer should do next*?

Second: the end-to-end principle rests on the line that any network "will be subject to failures of transmission at some statistically determined rate", and so integrity has to live in the end systems. Give me one change to the world that should make you drop end-to-end — and one change that should leave it exactly where it stands.
transcript.author:
Broadly right, with one correction worth making explicit. "Rough consensus and running code" (§2.4) describes how the *evolution happened* — that's the descriptive claim. The principles in §3–§6 are guidance for whoever designs or evaluates a protocol next — the normative claim. §1 says they're a snapshot, "in no way... a formal or invariant reference model." So the document is both, and the normative claim borrows its authority from the descriptive one. For your purposes, we're testing the normative claim.

On end-to-end: it stands on two prongs — Saltzer's knowledge argument (the function needs the application's help) and my failure-rate argument. To make me drop it, you'd have to defeat both: links reliable enough that the failure prong vanishes, *and* a network holding knowledge the endpoints lack and acting on it correctly. Today's QoS, multicast and mobility are partial, imperfect attempts at the second. Note §2.3 already concedes the network keeps some state — routes, QoS, compression histories — but insists it be self-healing and minimal. So end-to-end never meant a stateless network.

What leaves it exactly where it stands: new transmission media and faster links. §2.2 requires the internet layer to be independent of the hardware medium; bandwidth changes neither who holds knowledge nor who bears failure. Scale is the same — "millions of sites" (§3.3) is a stress test, not a refutation.

transcript.reader:
Two more, both aimed at where the holding is thinnest.

1. You've just told me the normative claim borrows its authority from the descriptive one — the principles are "found useful in the past", "a snapshot", "in no way a formal or invariant reference model" (§1). A hedge like that swallows every failure: whatever goes wrong, the snapshot just aged. So what would count as these principles being *wrong*, rather than merely becoming out of date? Name one reading we could actually look at that would show a §3–§6 principle was the wrong call when it was made — and name one that would leave it standing.

2. §2.2 puts up the ideal — one and only one protocol at the internet level — and then lists two reasons more than one might be in use, and notes that large private networks run several successfully. Let me swap that limit for a near neighbour. Suppose the ideal were "two internet-layer protocols, permanently: one for the public Internet, one for private internets." Which requirement in §3–§6 does that break? If nothing there breaks, is "one and only one" held by anything, or is it a preference dressed as a principle?
transcript.author:
**Q1.** Fair charge: §1's hedge could immunise everything. So draw the line. A principle is *wrong when made* if its supporting reasoning failed on evidence then available and the harm was foreseeable; it is merely *aged* if new facts invalidated a claim sound on the old ones. Only the second is covered by "snapshot."

Candidate: §4.3, case-independent ASCII public names. A reading that would falsify it: show that by 1996 global deployment already required non-ASCII names, that DNS names are a structural commitment rather than a parametric choice, and that §5.4 in the same document already committed to full internationalisation. Then the conflict was internal and knowable, and ASCII-only names were a wrong call, not an aged one — §3.7 ("almost complete solution now") won't excuse it, because DNS isn't revisable in place the way a parametric choice is.

A reading that leaves it standing: §4.3 constrains wire syntax — unambiguous, case-independent comparison — not the user's language. Localisation layers above it; IDNA/Punycode later did exactly that, leaving the ASCII wire format intact. On that reading §4.3 did what a wire-format rule should.

I lean to "standing." But the §5.4 tension is real, and I won't pretend §1's hedge dissolves it.

**Q2.** It breaks §3.2 if the two protocols "do the same thing." But if the private protocol serves genuinely different requirements, §2.2's own second caveat — "fundamentally new requirements" — already admits it, and nothing in §3–§6 breaks: §3.1 heterogeneity favours it, §3.3 is indifferent, §4.4 holds inside each scope. §4.5 and §6.1 strain only if traffic crosses a translator mid-path or the new protocol must fit the *IP* security architecture.

So the honest answer: "one and only one" is held by nothing in §3–§6. It isn't derived from any testable rule; it rests on §2.1's goal — connectivity, and "uniform and relatively seamless operations." Note the document's own register: "It is generally felt that…" That is consensus opinion, not stated principle.

So: a preference, yes — but a principled one, because permanent fragmentation at the internet layer degrades exactly the property §2.1 prizes. I defend it on purpose, not as a rule.

transcript.reader:
Two more — one about whether a part does any work, one about two parts that may be fighting.

1. §2.4 says engineering feedback from real implementations is more important than any architectural principles, and §3.14 says nothing gets standardised until there are multiple instances of running code. If that's so, which job do the §3–§6 principles do that running code doesn't do already? Name one change to the world where running code and a principle here would pull in opposite directions, and tell me which of the two wins in that case. If no change on the list can separate them, the principles are there for something other than steering — say what.

2. §2.3 wants the network's state "self-healing", "minimized", and lists QoS guarantees, session information and compression histories among the state it does keep; §3.10 wants us parsimonious with unsolicited packets, especially multicasts. Meanwhile §1 names multimedia and QoS as the very triggers for the next change. Push one side — more QoS and multicast, more of that state — and does the other side give way? Where is your line between "minimized state" and "enough state", and what reading would show you the line sits in the wrong place?
transcript.author:
**Q1.** Running code shows what *works*; the principles constrain what to *try*, and say what counts as proof. §3.14 is itself a principle — it defines the gate, and a gate can't be the thing it admits. Also, code can't speak to futures: whether to foreclose an option (§3.6), whether a design scales before you can afford to deploy it at scale (§3.3). And they're the shared vocabulary for rough consensus — §2.4's mechanism needs something to reach consensus *about*.

Opposite pull: §5.1, prefer unpatented technology. Deployed running code used patented algorithms; §3.14 says standardise what runs. Which wins? In practice, running code wins admission to the standards process, but §5.1 wins the *blessing* — it decides which running code gets called a standard. So neither is absolute; they gate different stages. That's the answer to your last clause too: if no change on the list separates them, the principles aren't steering so much as *legitimating* — supplying the reasoned basis for choices the community would otherwise make by weight of deployment alone.

**Q2.** Push QoS and multicast and §3.10 gives way first — it says "parsimonious", not "never", and in-network replication is genuinely cheaper than endpoint duplication. That's why multicast exists.

§2.3's line is harder. My line: state is acceptable when it is (a) derivable automatically, not manually configured — that last sentence is the real constraint; (b) self-healing; (c) amortised over many flows rather than per-flow; (d) whose loss degrades rather than disconnects.

What shows the line wrong: measurement that per-flow state at every hop beats endpoint recovery on cost — RSVP/IntServ was the live test, and it lost on scaling; DiffServ moved the state to edges. Conversely, if some dominant class made in-network state provably cheaper end-to-end, "minimized" would have to yield to §3.4 (performance and cost) and §3.7. I'd accept that reading. I won't pretend the line is fixed — §1 says it isn't.

transcript.reader:
Two more.

1. Let me build the strongest rival properly. Rival: the Internet looks this way not because §3–§6 guided it, but because deployment economics, accidents and vendor weight selected what survived; the principles are a tidy account of the winners written after the fact. What change to the world would make the two give *different* answers — a case where principles-first and deployment-first would have predicted different architectures, at a moment when you could look? If nothing could have separated them, say so, and tell me whether the document is an explanation or a souvenir.

2. Flip §1. It says constant change is "perhaps the only principle of the Internet that should survive indefinitely." Suppose the technology had instead been stable for 25 years — one quiet decade after another. What would the document have said, and would the same move have produced "stability is the only lasting principle" just as smoothly? If the same reasoning covers both outcomes, what does that leave "constant change" ruling out?
transcript.author:
**Q1.** Real separator, and it was visible: datagrams versus virtual circuits at the internet layer. Deployment-first predicted X.25-style virtual circuits — carriers, PTTs, installed switching plant, vendor weight all pointed there, and OSI embodied it. Principles-first, from §2.3's fate-sharing and end-to-end reasoning, predicted connectionless datagrams. Around 1978–81 you could look, and they diverged. Principles won that fork, against deployment pressure. That is the strongest evidence the document isn't a souvenir.

But deployment won others: NAT persisted despite §2.2 and §4.5, and IPv4 exhaustion outran IPv6. So: partial explanation with real steering effect — an explanation, not just a souvenir, but not a complete one. I won't claim §3–§6 determined outcomes; on the evidence they intermittently outvoted deployment weight, which is weaker than "guided."

**Q2.** No, it wouldn't have said that — and that's the point. §1's argument is an induction from observed rates of change; with no observed change the induction isn't available, so you wouldn't get "stability lasts" by the same route. But you could: "principles that worked have kept working." The move is symmetric, and cheap — which is the tell. If the same reasoning yields both "everything changes" and "everything persists," then "constant change" predicts nothing about the technology.

What it does rule out is narrower and real: it forbids treating any *specific* principle as invariant. §1 says exactly that — "not... to lay down dogma." So "constant change" is a meta-rule about humility, not an empirical forecast. As a forecast it's unfalsifiable and I should concede that; as a discipline on the rest of the document it does work.

transcript.reader:
Two more.

1. §3.9, "be strict when sending and tolerant when receiving": was that worked out from the problem itself, or fitted on the interoperability failures you'd met — and what has it never met? Here's a case it hadn't met in 1996: receivers tolerant enough to accept malformed-but-common input froze bad behaviour into the wire format, so the strictness never got adopted and the format could not be changed — what later got called ossification. Does that break §3.9, narrow it, or leave it standing? Say where we'd look to tell those apart.

2. Two clauses in §6 that may be pulling: §6.3, permiting alternative algorithms so long as each is explicitly labelled, and §6.5, mandating one algorithm or suite so that any two endpoints can negotiate a secure context. Make §6.3 stronger — allow any strong algorithm — and does §6.5 give way? At what point do the two fail together? And what reading would show the line you draw between them sits in the wrong place?
transcript.author:
**Q1.** Fitted, not derived — it's Postel's maxim, earned by meeting incomplete implementations. What it never met: deviations that were *incentive-driven* rather than accidental, and attackers who are thin receivers on purpose.

Your ossification case doesn't leave it standing as written. The tolerance prong, applied undifferentiated, produces the outcome it was meant to prevent: interop now, immovable format forever. So §3.9 *narrows* — the sending prong survives intact ("follow specifications precisely when sending" is exactly right), the receiving prong needs a qualifier: tolerate only what the specification permits, and specify behaviour for undefined input.

Where to look to tell narrowing from breaking: (a) did the protocol carry §3.12 self-describing objects, version numbers, explicit extension points? If yes, tolerance is cheap and reversible and the principle holds; if no, every tolerated quirk becomes permanent, and it breaks. (b) Does the spec say what to do with malformed input, or say nothing and let receivers improvise? Silence is what ossifies. The later community revision — be strict about what you accept unless the spec says otherwise, and watch for what's actually on the wire — is a narrowing, not a repudiation.

**Q2.** Strengthen §6.3 to "any strong algorithm" and §6.5 doesn't collapse immediately — it only needs *some* common member. But it gives way if "any" replaces "a mandated one," because nothing then guarantees the intersection is non-empty.

They fail together in two spots. First, unauthenticated labelling: an attacker strips strength labels, forcing the weakest common algorithm; §6.3's explicit labelling is defeated *and* §6.5's negotiation becomes the downgrade vector — there's a secure context, just not a strong one. Second, a singleton mandated suite that cryptanalysis breaks: §6.5's guarantee is common-mode void at once, and §6.3's alternatives are unreachable because peers share only that one. So the joint failure point is exactly unauthenticated negotiation plus a non-revisable mandatory set.

Where to look: IANA registry revision history and whether a weak mandated algorithm was ever withdrawn promptly; whether negotiation is authenticated against downgrade; whether any two conformant implementations can still find one common *strong* algorithm after the floor breaks.

I draw the line at "mandated to implement," not "mandated to use" — a revisable interop floor, with agreement up from there. A reading showing my line wrong: a floor broken by cryptanalysis faster than the community revises it makes the floor the attack surface; conversely, if implementations hardcode rather than negotiate, the floor is too rigid and §6.3's agility is nominal.

transcript.reader:
Last two from me.

1. NAT is the case your own document's principles were meant to forbid, and it persisted. §4.5 says addresses are the same at start and finish of transmission; §4.4 says an address is unique within any scope where it may appear; §2.2 says one protocol at the internet layer; §2.3 says in-network state must be minimal and self-healing. A NAT box holds per-flow translation state that is neither self-healing nor derivable without watching the flow, and it rewrites §4.5's addresses. So: which part of §2–§4 gave way to absorb it — was a patch added, was the claim quietly narrowed, or were the principles simply left failing? Was the narrowing said out loud at the time? And what would you measure to see whether that state is swallowing a job that end-to-end was supposed to keep?

2. §5.2 asserts that all the technology needed to implement Internet standards can be fabricated in each country, so export controls are only of secondary importance. That is a factual claim doing real work in the argument. Name the change to the world that would have shown it wrong in 1996, and where you would have looked — and if it had been wrong, would §5.2 have become a new claim, recorded as one?
transcript.author:
**Q1.** NAT predates this RFC — Egevang and Francis, RFC 1631, May 1994 — and §2–§4 don't mention it anywhere. That omission is mine, and it's the strongest single count against the document.

Which gave way? Mostly nothing was patched; the principles were left failing. What was spoken aloud came later and was a *narrowing of scope*, not a revision: RFC 2663 (1999) introduced "address realm," and RSIP (RFC 3105, 2001) formalised addresses as unique per realm — which quietly rescopes §4.4's "any scope where they may appear." §4.5 was not narrowed; it was documented as violated, in RFC 2993 (2000), as an architectural complaint rather than a sanctioned change. So: §4.5 left failing, §4.4 narrowed out loud a few years late, §2.3 conceded implicitly. I'd rather say that plainly than dress it as evolution.

To measure whether NAT state is swallowing end-to-end's job: fraction of flows whose continuity is coupled to a middlebox's liveness but not the endpoints' — that is fate-sharing, measured directly. Second, deployment latency: time from a new transport spec to working end-to-end without middlebox upgrades. Third, and sharpest: how much new protocol work goes to traversal rather than function. And whether translation needs application-layer gateways — an ALG means the network is doing a job requiring endpoint knowledge, which is the violation in kind, not degree.

**Q2.** One counterexample would have sufficed: a standard mandating an algorithm whose design was not public. The Escrowed Encryption Standard did exactly that — Skipjack was classified, so no country could fabricate it from the specification. That makes §5.2 false as a factual claim, not merely optimistic.

Where to have looked: for each proposed standard, is the algorithm publicly specified and free of sole-source components? Classification or a single licensed supplier breaks it.

Had it been wrong, it would have to become a new claim: prefer designs whose implementation is publicly specifiable, and treat exportability as evidence of that, not a thing to be discounted. And the community did eventually record something adjacent and explicit — the IETF's 2000 policy declining to make wiretapping a design requirement. So yes: the honest outcome is a replacement claim, recorded, not a quiet edit to §5.2.

report:
# Hard-to-vary report: RFC 1958, "Architectural Principles of the Internet"

## 1. The question, frozen

What the document's title and opening make central is the *normative* claim: what a designer or evaluator of an Internet protocol should do, and why. The owner confirmed this, and added that the normative claim borrows its authority from the descriptive one (§2: the architecture evolved, no Grand Plan). Range: the public Internet as of 1996. Kind of question: mostly "does it achieve its purpose", with a "what produces it" claim underneath. The jobs the owner named are the triggers in §1 — IPv4 scaling limits, gigabit/multimedia, QoS and security guarantees. Jobs I added are marked as mine.

## 2. The explanation in parts

Taken in the owner's words: connectivity is the goal, IP is the tool, intelligence is end-to-end (§2.1); one and only one protocol at the internet layer, independent of hardware (§2.2); end-to-end, fate-sharing, datagrams over virtual circuits, network state minimal and self-healing (§2.3); running code over principles (§2.4); a set of design rules (§3); name and address rules (§4); external rules (§5); security rules (§6); and constant change as the one lasting principle (§1).

## 3. Part by part

| Part | Mark | What holds it, or what would replace it |
|---|---|---|
| §2.1 connectivity / IP / end-to-end | Held | By the 1978–81 datagram-vs-virtual-circuit fork, where principles-first and deployment-first gave different answers and could be checked. |
| §2.2 one and only one internet-layer protocol | Loose | Swap in "two, permanently, serving different requirement sets" — nothing in §3–§6 breaks (owner agrees). Its two caveats are a catch-all with no gauge. |
| §2.3 end-to-end, fate-sharing, minimal state | Held | By the fate-sharing job. Gauge: share of flows whose continuity depends on a middlebox's liveness, not the endpoints'. |
| §2.4 running code beats principles | Held if | Only by the job "principles steer what to try" — in doubt, since deployment overrode them at NAT and IPv4/IPv6. |
| §3.14 no standard without running code | Held | By the admission job. §5.1 does the blessing job; the patent case showed the two are separate. |
| §3.9 strict send / tolerant receive | Held (send); Held if (receive) | The tolerance prong is held only by the interop job, now in doubt: tolerance froze malformed behaviour into formats. Owner's qualifier is a new claim. |
| §3.2, §3.3, §3.5, §3.11, §3.12 | Held | Each by a named job: duplication cost; millions of sites; simplest working solution; the routing-vs-DNS circular dependency is a job a change would break. |
| §4.3 case-independent ASCII names | Held | By the wire-syntax job (unambiguous, case-independent comparison), with a stated limit above it. Pulls against §5.4. |
| §4.4 unique within scope | Held if | Its scope was re-scoped years later ("address realm"). That is a new claim, recorded late. |
| §4.5 same address at start and finish | Held if | Held only by the end-to-end job, which NAT outvoted. No patch was made; the violation was documented, not sanctioned. |
| §5.1 prefer unpatented technology | Held | By the blessing job. |
| §5.2 export controls secondary | Held if | Held only by "no country holds a choke point". The owner's own counterexample (a standard mandating a classified algorithm) defeats it; his replacement is a new claim. |
| §6.2 confidentiality is the user's job | Held | By the end-to-end job; the stated limit carries its reason inside it. |
| §6.3 labelled alternatives / §6.5 one mandated algorithm | Held / Held | Agility and interop. They pull: widen §6.3 to "any strong algorithm" and §6.5 fails where negotiation is unauthenticated or the mandated set cannot be revised. |
| §1 constant change | Idle as a forecast; Held if as a discipline | Swap it for "stability lasts" and nothing else changes; only the "forbid dogma" job holds it. The "snapshot" hedge is a catch-all; its gauge came out in conversation, not in the text. |

## 4. Whole-explanation checks

**Flip.** §1 covers both outcomes: the owner conceded the same move yields "stability is the only lasting principle", so as a forecast it rules out nothing. §2.4 flips too: had the principles been ignored and things worked, running code would have got the credit.

**Direction.** The rules run forward, but their authority runs backward, from what survived. The owner names one real forward test (the datagram fork) and one failure (NAT). "Intermittently outvoted deployment" is his own phrase, and it is weaker than the document's register suggests.

**Answer in the starting points.** §1's "connectivity is its own reward" and §3.14's gate are both starting point and evidence. The fork keeps this from being pure circularity, but not by much.

**Pairs that pull.** §6.3/§6.5 (owner draws the line at "mandated to implement, not to use"). §4.3/§5.4 pull with nothing resolving them. §2.3's minimal state pulls against the QoS guarantees §2.3 also lists, and §3.10 gives way first.

**Catch-alls and gauges.** "Snapshot, not invariant" (gauge supplied late); "minimized" state (gauges named: RSVP, DiffServ); "fundamentally new requirements" in §2.2 (no gauge at all).

**Left off the change list.** Middleboxes and NAT above all; mobility; multicast; the commercial and regulatory environment. The owner called NAT's absence the strongest single count against the document.

**Rival.** "The principles are a souvenir of what deployment happened to select." Separated, partly, by the fork — and the owner accepts the verdict is "partial, not complete".

**Provenance.** §3.9 is fitted, and met a case it was never fitted on. §5.2 is asserted, and known false in 1996. §2.3's fate-sharing is built: it commits about cases nobody has tried.

## 5. What would make it harder to vary

1. Write the owner's own gauge — wrong-when-made versus merely aged — into §1, and apply it to §2.2 and §5.2, the two parts with no gauge.
2. Put the middlebox case into §2–§4 and state the narrowed claim out loud, with the fate-sharing gauge as the measure. That is the one counter-case the list leaves out, and the principles fail on it.

## 6. What this does not show

Passing is not truth. Several parts above were narrowed or replaced *during this conversation* — §3.9's tolerance prong, §4.4's scope, §5.2 — and each is a new claim made now, not a repair of the 1996 text.

## 7. One next step

Take §2.2. Write down the change that would show "one and only one" is wrong, and what you would measure — the owner already concedes no §3–§6 rule holds it.
